title: An Automated Virtual Reality Training System for Teacher-Student Interaction: A Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI-enhanced virtual reality (VR) system can teach the steps of a nondirective mathematical questioning strategy more effectively than conventional instruction alone. The motivation is the lack of qualified supervisors and time/resources for rehearsal-based teacher preparation, especially for interaction-focused skills that are hard to practice with traditional lecture-only formats.

The intervention combined recorded lecture and video modeling with automated VR rehearsal. In the experimental condition, participants first received the same didactic lecture as the control group, then completed VR-based error-free prompting and delayed prompting sessions in which the system used speech recognition and automated classification to present prompts, score responses, and provide feedback. The control group received only the lecture and modeling, followed by the same observed mastery probes without VR practice. The outcome measures included observed performance on lesson steps, automated versus human assessment correspondence, confidence ratings, and generalization/maintenance probes.

The study recruited 30 University of Iowa undergraduate and graduate students who were not expected to be highly familiar with mathematics education. Participants were randomly assigned to intervention or control groups and were assessed over three weekly sessions in a face-to-face small-room setting. Results showed that both groups improved after instruction, but the VR group performed significantly better on posttest, maintenance, and generalization measures and reported slightly higher confidence. The automated assessments corresponded closely with human observations. The authors conclude that automated VR can deliver effective, evidence-based training with limited instructor management, though they note the need for broader validation and evidence of transfer to authentic practice.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a clear comparison group, baseline equivalence, and repeated measures, but the sample is small (n=30) and the intervention is tightly scoped to a single training task. There are also some concerns about generalizability because participants were university students rather than target education personnel.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a large improvement in procedural performance (d=1.334 at posttest; d=1.39 at maintenance), which exceeds the threshold for a high-impact finding. Effects were observed on a relevant training outcome for education personnel, though the population and task are narrow.

interventions.use_case: AI-augmented virtual reality simulation for behavioral skills training in teacher-student interaction, specifically rehearsing a nondirective mathematical questioning strategy with automated speech recognition, classification, prompts, and feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The AI-enhanced VR training improved participants' performance on a nondirective mathematical questioning procedure compared with lecture and modeling alone. At posttest, the intervention group scored 88% (SD 22.62%, n=15) versus 63.33% (SD 22.64%, n=15) in control, t(28)=3.653, p<.001, d=1.334; at maintenance, the intervention group remained higher at 83.33% (SD 24.40%) versus 54.67% (SD 15.98%), t(28)=3.807, p<.001, d=1.39.
finding.measure: Observed mastery probe (OMP) percentage of correct steps in the mathematical questioning procedure; maintenance probe performance

finding.finding_summary: Participants receiving VR rehearsal reported higher confidence in using the procedure at maintenance than the control group, although this effect was small and became non-significant after multiple-comparison correction. The reported comparison was U=64, p=.04, Cohen r=0.137, indicating only a modest confidence gain.
